title: Trade, climate, and conflict shocks reach households through income, food, and unequal exposure channels
source_unit: World Bank, Trade Policy and Natural Shocks Dashboard, with methodology reference to Crops, Conflict, and Climate Change
geography: Low- and middle-income countries and more than 50 countries represented in the World Bank interactive household-shock dashboard

denominator.unit: World Bank modeled household-income shock scenario

real_income_loss.unit: percent forecast reduction in real incomes associated with changes in yields due to climate change

transmission.value: The dashboard traces natural and policy-driven shocks through household income, food security, and other economic channels

observations.method: World Bank interactive dashboard using modeled natural-shock and household-distribution channels; the page points to a Policy Research Working Paper for methodology.
observations.uncertainty: The 11.99% estimate is a model-based scenario, not a realized national income change or a causal estimate for every household; shock definitions, elasticities, and time horizons determine the result.
observations.subgroup: Households in countries exposed to climate-related yield changes, differentiated by income and economic channel in the dashboard.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adaptation, trade substitution, irrigation, crop changes, transfers, and local resilience can reduce realized losses; modeled exposure is not realized hardship.

denominator.unit: World Bank modeled low- and middle-income-country household-income shock scenario

real_income_loss.unit: percent average reduction in real household incomes associated with war-induced food inflation from restrictive grain and fertilizer export policies

food_security_route.value: Export restrictions transmit conflict through food prices and household purchasing power

observations.method: World Bank dashboard summary of modeled household welfare impacts from war-induced food inflation and restrictive trade policies.
observations.uncertainty: The 2.90% figure is an average modeled effect across low- and middle-income countries, not a direct observation of household income or a uniform country estimate; the dashboard does not establish one policy’s causal contribution in every setting.
observations.subgroup: Households in low- and middle-income countries exposed to food-price increases, especially food-insecure and lower-income households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Domestic production, targeted transfers, food substitution, inventories, and alternative suppliers can buffer food-price transmission; export restrictions may also be adopted for domestic political or food-security reasons.

observations.period: 2025 dashboard; unequal exposure and household response

denominator.unit: countries represented in the dashboard visualization and household-shock comparisons

distributional_heterogeneity.value: Welfare impacts vary enormously across the income distribution, with already vulnerable households bearing the brunt of the costs

dashboard_scope.value: The dashboard visualizes variation across households, economic channels, and household responses in more than 50 countries

observations.method: World Bank interactive visualization of modeled household exposure and response pathways across countries and income distributions.
observations.uncertainty: The dashboard’s cross-household comparisons depend on model inputs, survey or distributional data, and scenario assumptions; it does not provide a longitudinal record of the same households’ adaptations or recovery.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income and otherwise vulnerable households, compared with households at different positions in the income distribution and across countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Vulnerability can be offset by public transfers, informal support, asset ownership, local production, or substitution, so income position alone does not determine realized welfare loss.

observations.period: 2025 dashboard; policy and natural shocks as one household-risk system

shock_set.value: The dashboard combines natural, anthropogenic, and policy-driven shocks, including climate-yield changes, conflict-linked food inflation, and restrictive trade policies

policy_relevance.value: The same shock can operate through income, food security, prices, production, trade, and household response channels

observations.method: World Bank policy visualization linking trade policy, climate and conflict shocks, household distribution, and response channels.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies plausible transmission routes but does not prove that every channel activates in every country or that a specific policy intervention improves welfare.
observations.subgroup: Households, food systems, farmers, consumers, governments, and trade-policy institutions in shock-exposed countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: A policy that raises short-term prices can protect longer-term supply or domestic production; welfare evaluation requires timing, incidence, substitution, and recovery rather than a single immediate loss estimate.

related_sources.claim: World Bank methodology reference linked from the dashboard for Crops, Conflict, and Climate Change; access is subject to the document server’s delivery behavior.
World Bank poverty and climate context for household vulnerability and shock transmission.

boundary: This record adds a modeled household-distribution layer to the trade, climate, food, and geopolitical-shock map. It is an interactive World Bank analytical dashboard, not respondent-level longitudinal data, a realized household-income panel, a universal causal estimate, or proof that any specific trade restriction caused a measured welfare loss in a named country.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank dashboard page was reviewed for climate-yield income loss, war-induced food-inflation income loss, distributional heterogeneity, country coverage, channels, and household responses. The dashboard page and its linked methodology reference were retained; the underlying interactive data are not claimed as a local respondent-level extract.
